memory_update.text: New Hotspots should be handled as a cross-sector chokepoint funnel: breaking policy/trade shocks plus demand acceleration can reveal shared upstream constraints before standard sector labels capture them.
Tungsten APT/WF6 is a candidate hidden semiconductor-industrial-defense bottleneck; later layers should verify customs data, non-China processing capacity and public supplier exposure.
Sulphur/sulphuric acid is a candidate feedstock chokepoint linking copper SX-EW, Indonesian HPAL nickel and fertilizers; later layers should map acid supply, logistics and smelter byproduct flows.
HBM/advanced-packaging discovery should move below the obvious memory-producer layer into tools, consumables, inspection, test and thermal materials, with strict proof of customer linkage.
AI data-center power should be decomposed into power availability, switchgear, transformers, cooling, interconnection, EPC and regional utility constraints rather than only semiconductor demand.
Marine biofouling/coatings is a speculative second-order shipping-disruption lane; useful for obscure supplier discovery but requires stronger order or regulatory evidence before promotion.

Layer 1B should build a 40-80 company universe across the six nodes, including market cap, analyst coverage, source-backed exposure, revenue materiality, customer concentration and falsification triggers.

summary: Initial Serenity Layer 1A decomposition for 'New Hotspots': treat the theme as a breaking-news supply-chain shock funnel rather than a single sector. The strongest early lanes from the provided evidence are: tungsten/APT/WF6 disruption affecting semiconductors, tooling and defense; sulphur/sulphuric-acid disruption cascading into copper, nickel and fertilizers; HBM/advanced-packaging second-layer suppliers where obvious producers are already well-covered; data-center power and grid infrastructure as a demand shock from AI buildout; nuclear fuel/components as a policy-and-power bottleneck; and marine biofouling/coatings as a second-order shipping-disruption beneficiary. This is not a security recommendation. The purpose is to define nodes for later evidence collection, public-market mapping, and falsification.

theme_map.public_market_search_strategy: Run a two-lane funnel. Lane 1 uses reference leaders only to define demand reality and capex direction: hyperscalers, AI accelerators, memory leaders, major foundries, grid equipment leaders and large nuclear/power companies. Lane 2 searches one or two steps upstream or sideways for underfollowed public suppliers: specialty chemical processors, semiconductor gases, testing/inspection, advanced-packaging consumables, power-component suppliers, uranium/enrichment/nuclear-service bottlenecks, vessel-maintenance/coatings suppliers, logistics data providers and regional industrial companies with hidden customer dependencies. Prefer companies with explicit revenue linkage, constrained capacity, customer qualification, regulatory licensing or scarce processing assets. Avoid ranking securities at Layer 1A; only define search lanes and falsification paths.
supply_side_constraints: Critical minerals may share a single intermediate processing choke point even when downstream industries appear separate.
Export bans and quota reductions can convert regional commodity tightness into global industrial bottlenecks.
Qualified semiconductor materials and gases face long customer qualification cycles and limited supplier bases.
Advanced packaging and HBM supply chains are already partly priced at the producer level, so discovery must move one or two layers down.
Power infrastructure bottlenecks include transformer lead times, grid interconnection queues, turbine capacity, nuclear fuel availability and construction execution risk.
Physical shipping disruption can create non-obvious operational bottlenecks such as hull fouling, cleaning capacity, coatings supply, fuel burn and regulatory compliance.
